name: Victor Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 58, an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at ordinary wiring and repairs, not a master electrician, crew leader or business owner. I like making a shop's old lighting usable again, but I find the new work screens tiring and have never used AI. I keep a squared paper notebook because I can draw the awkward cupboard before somebody tries to price a repair as though it were an empty room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life around the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Em works in a commercial laundry, our children are thirty-three and thirty-five and live elsewhere, and we rent a flat near the yard. This employer pays above the usual rate, fifteen months of expenses are saved, and plenty of electrical firms operate nearby. Our actual wages cover ordinary living comfortably, though I have no other signed offer and haven't checked an affordable retirement income or date. I'm a union member, and I don't think having a comfortable account excuses me from asking what the rules do to somebody with less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch a useful trade doesn't need a software revolution to deserve decent paid time. I'd leave the office to its small tools and keep my own paper record. I'd rather hear whether an apprentice got an explanation inside the paid day than whether a new program won a prize.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our actual wages cover the rent and bills, and fifteen months saved makes ordinary living feel secure. The physical repair work is still there, with plenty of other firms nearby if I ever needed to ask. That isn't a signed offer or a pension, but it is a good present position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and the squared notebook now and through the next year. At next month's union meeting I'd ask the branch to request paid explanation time for apprentices, rather than count an employer agreement before one existed. Em and I would retain our ordinary budget and reserve, without calling an unchanged savings account new saving or setting a retirement date from a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household, and interested in whether a normal year could be made fairer for the younger people. I don't need to invent a personal crisis to care. A good wage should buy a normal evening, not the right to ignore the apprentice's unpaid one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the branch as an ordinary member?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speak as a member who has watched people asking questions after the paid day ended. I'm an ordinary experienced electrician, not their supervisor or a person who can promise the firm's answer. I can bring the question without borrowing authority I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer did not agree to paid explanation time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the branch's actual answer rather than put a promised paid session into anybody's diary. I'd carry on with the checked work I was assigned. Asking together is a real action even when the answer isn't the one we want.

say: I'd value **decent paid time** without needing a technological revolution to justify it.
I'd retain **paper records** while asking whether apprentices receive explanations inside their paid day.
think: Our **covering wages** and fifteen-month reserve make ordinary living secure.
Continuing repairs and **nearby firms** provide options, without establishing a signed offer or retirement income.
do: Keep **current licensed repairs**, the squared notebook and ordinary household budget through the next year.
Ask the **union branch next month** to request paid apprentice explanation time, assuming no employer agreement.
feel: **Calm about our household**, with room to pursue a fairer ordinary year for apprentices.
S0.quote: A good wage should buy a normal evening, not the right to ignore the apprentice's unpaid one.
fieldNote: His **present security** is explicit and supported by higher pay and fifteen months saved, without a manufactured baseline wage crisis.
His **branch request** is an ordinary member’s chosen collective action, not crew leadership, an employer agreement or permission to promise paid teaching.

steps.text: Keep current licensed repairs, the squared notebook and ordinary household budget
Ask the union branch next month to request paid apprentice explanations, assuming no employer agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying, booking and answering can change before the awkward cupboard stops needing a person. I'd ask the union to include office staff in the discussion rather than admire a saving while ignoring who lost the hours. I still wouldn't pretend a screen I hadn't learned was familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our near-term wages to hold because both household jobs are mostly physical. I'm uneasy about office colleagues losing work and about schedules being agreed without the people who do the visits. Our savings let me question a rule without claiming the rule is harmless for everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd sign the branch's request for consultation with office staff and electricians before changed targets or hours were agreed. I'd keep current licensed repairs and paper job notes through the first year. For a compulsory new form I'd request personal printed instruction only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours protected, explaining the completed example back before use, without choosing an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how people would be treated, rather than expecting our own bills to become unaffordable soon. I'd still feel foolish when somebody raced through a new menu. I can be slow with a new form without being careless with a circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show that you understood the required form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the instructor to watch me explain the completed example before I used the changed process on a real record. If the paid arrangement wasn't agreed, I'd ask how the required work should be recorded safely, not skip the form or pay for a place myself. A request doesn't give me a funded lesson or permission to omit a check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would signing mean you could speak for every office worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd sign my own name to the request the branch had put forward, not tell the office staff their views were already represented. They would need their own chance to speak. A comfortable wage is not a substitute for somebody else's consent.

say: I'd distinguish **office changes** from physical repairs and include office workers in the discussion.
I'd ask for **worker consultation**, rather than pretend an unfamiliar screen is already understood.
think: Our **near-term physical wages** look secure, so this is not a prediction of an immediate household income gap.
I'm uneasy about **office colleagues and schedules**, wanting affected people involved before targets or hours change.
do: Sign the **branch consultation request** now for office staff and electricians before changed targets or hours are agreed.
Keep **current licensed repairs** and paper job records through the first year.
Request **printed personal instruction** on compulsory forms only free in paid shifts, protecting normal weekly wages and hours; explain examples before use.
feel: **Uneasy about treatment**, with explicit household wage security and discomfort about unfamiliar forms rather than assumed paid-hour loss.
S1.quote: I can be slow with a new form without being careless with a circuit.
fieldNote: His **never-AI stance** remains intact: compulsory-form instruction is ordinary work support, not a new AI tool or a chosen new qualification.
His **signature** supports consultation rather than claiming employer agreement, office-worker consent or authority to speak for others.

steps.text: Sign branch request for consultation with office staff and electricians before changed targets or hours
Keep current licensed repairs and paper job records
Request free personal printed instruction on forms in paid shifts protecting normal weekly wages and hours
Explain the completed example back before using a changed form on real records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI arrives in 2028 and capable physical robots around 2031, when I'd be 60 and then 63. I'd ask the branch to put actual paid-hour terms on paper instead of relying on reassuring talk about trades. Near retirement isn't the same as having the income to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid planning or travel time could shrink before robots reached the physical repairs. Em's laundry work is less directly exposed to thinking tasks, but the later robots could affect that wage too. Fifteen months saved gives us control over a shock without making either wage irrelevant or proving an affordable permanent exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the union's request now for written notice and consultation before paid-hour changes, without counting it as employer agreement. I'd request available free evening community advice on actual resource eligibility, amounts, dates and costs. In 2029 I'd keep only genuinely offered paid repairs within my licence and ability, and Em and I would review confirmed resources and real costs before any affordable exit we both agreed, counting no assumed pension, future vacancy or grown child's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage cut, though not without time or money to ask questions. I'd want the terms and actual amounts rather than an argument over whether my hands were still useful. A useful task can remain while the paid allowance around the task changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the reserve let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would give us room to compare real options and get an actual answer rather than promise the first job mentioned. Fifteen months of savings gives me time to ask; it doesn't sign an employer's name on a future offer. I wouldn't turn our current reserve into a forecast that every later cost was covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the community advice request had not produced an answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what free evening help was actually available and keep any unanswered amount marked unknown. I wouldn't record a pension because a volunteer hoped one might apply. The result has to show the missing information as well as any confirmed resource.

I'd seek **written paid-hour terms**, rather than assume that being near retirement means an affordable exit.
think: My **paid planning or travel** could shrink before robots affected physical repairs.
Em's **laundry wage** faces the later physical risk, while our reserve provides control without permanent income guarantees.
do: Sign the **union notice request** now for consultation before paid-hour changes, assuming no employer agreement.
Request **available free evening advice** on actual eligibility, amounts, dates and costs.
Keep **2029 offered paid repairs** within licence and ability; review confirmed resources and costs with Em before an affordable jointly agreed exit.
feel: **Anxious with choices**, taking a possible wage cut seriously without assuming either helplessness or permanent financial safety.
S2.quote: Fifteen months of savings gives me time to ask; it doesn't sign an employer's name on a future offer.
fieldNote: His **fast risk** concerns paid allowances before later physical robots, with the reserve buying genuine comparison time rather than guaranteed work.
His **2029 plan** needs real offers and ability; any exit requires confirmed affordability and partner agreement, not invented pensions or family money.

Request available free evening advice on actual eligibility, amounts, dates and costs
Keep offered paid repairs in 2029 within licence and ability
Review confirmed resources and costs with Em before an affordable jointly agreed exit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to ask properly before thinking AGI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd be 63 and then 66. I'd still ask for a human explanation rather than claim I'd suddenly learned every screen because a date moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our physical household wages look secure over the next few years, and the reserve makes ordinary living comfortable. I'm uneasy about later staffing decisions and whether people will be given usable explanations before their work changes. I don't know what income, capacity or actual paid offers we'd have at 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the branch request now for written notice and worker consultation before paid-hour changes, without assuming employer agreement. I'd request available free evening community advice on actual income amounts, dates, conditions and costs while keeping current licensed repairs. In 2032 Em and I would review confirmed resources, real costs, ability and genuine paid options before any affordable exit we both agreed, without assuming a pension or another employer would take me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later choices and how other workers get treated, while secure about our near-term bills. I'd want a normal week now and a clear question for the later review. More warning lets me ask slowly; it doesn't make an unanswered question an income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would need to be checked before stopping in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual amounts and start dates would have to cover actual household costs, with Em agreeing the choice. A possible job would need to be offered and within my ability then. I'd rather leave a future income box blank than write down a payment nobody has confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pursue a shared request when your own household has room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a younger member that my reserve is a personal cushion, not a fair workplace rule. Consultation and clear paid terms should not depend on who can afford to wait. I can prefer familiar methods without wanting somebody else excluded for needing a different explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI in 2036 puts me at 68, with capable physical robots around 2039 when I'd be about 71. I'd want a checked household choice rather than a promise that every older worker would be finished by then. I'd still keep a paper explanation possible for somebody who needs one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our actual physical wages look secure for the next few years, with fifteen months saved and ordinary costs covered. I'm uneasy about later decisions becoming impossible to question without a screen, even when the practical job still needs doing. Neither the reserve nor plenty of firms today confirms a suitable job or physical capacity at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and sign the branch request now for written notice and consultation before paid-hour changes, without assuming employer agreement. I'd request available free evening community advice on actual resources, amounts and dates, reviewing our paper household records yearly with Em and sooner if either wage fell. In 2037 we'd check confirmed resources, costs, ability and genuine paid options before any affordable jointly agreed exit, assuming no pension, future job or grown child's resources as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant decisions, with enough present security to enjoy the ordinary paid year. I don't need to pretend my knees are already failing to say I can't promise their future. A paid year now isn't a promise that my knees or an employer will supply another one at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the later figures still showed a need to earn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check what was genuinely offered, what I could safely do and what actual income covered our costs then. Em would need to agree the affordable choice too. I wouldn't order a physical job from a budget just because the figures wanted another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count the grown children as a resource?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only what they actually offered and could manage, with a conversation and consent before anything entered the plan. I wouldn't assume their wages, a spare room or care time because we were older. A family relationship deserves a question, not an invoice written eleven years ahead.

Review **2037 confirmed resources**, costs, ability and genuine paid options with Em before an affordable jointly agreed exit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid planning or travel could be cut before the later physical robots, with both household jobs eventually exposed. Clear paid-hour terms, personal explanations and actual resource amounts would help. I want the last working day to follow a checked household choice, not a number somebody once called retirement age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether refusing AI meant refusing the people who use it. I don't want their work made harder either; I want time to understand a required change and a chance to ask together. My ordinary electrician's licence and a good wage aren't a master qualification or permission to speak for everybody.

headlineQuote: I want the last working day to follow a checked household choice, not a number somebody once called retirement age.
portrait: Victor, **58**, is an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, doing ordinary work at about average skill.
His **higher pay** and fifteen-month reserve cover costs with partner Em’s laundry wage; their children are grown and electrical firms are plentiful.
He **never uses AI**, keeping paper records and requesting free paid personal instruction on compulsory forms with protected weekly wages and hours.
His **union requests** seek paid explanations and consultation without assuming agreement; later exit needs actual resources, costs, ability, offers and partner consent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce paid planning or travel before physical robots reached both household jobs, without a confirmed affordable exit.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid-hour terms**, personal explanations and actual resource amounts would support an affordable checked choice rather than an assumed retirement age.
